narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order: your LSAT score, your class ranking after the third year of law school, and your undergraduate GPA. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and it pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other two factors. Your third-year class ranking was the second most important driver and it pushed the outcome strongly toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA also worked against you, though with less force than your class rank.

Compared with students who were accepted, you finished both your first and third years in a much lower decile (2 versus an average around 6), and your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 sits well below the 3.23 average of admitted students. Your family income and plan to attend full-time were typical and did not affect the result. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank through stronger academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT if you can increase your score meaningfully. These two changes would directly address the biggest reasons for the current rejection. (218 words)
